paragraphs.notes: Butler's 'mess' is a prepared dish or portion, a sense that is dead outside 'mess hall'. Today it reads as disorder or dirt. The thing is the kykeon (Od. 10.234-235: cheese, barley meal and honey stirred into Pramnian wine; named κυκεών at 10.290 and 10.316), which Butler's next sentence treats as a drink ('When they had drunk'). 'brew' is current English for a drink mixed from several ingredients. It keeps Butler's verb 'mixed', his 'with' and the whole list in his order. It does not announce the drug, so Butler's separate 'but she drugged it' keeps its force. In 'mixed them a brew', 'brew' reads as a concoction, not as slang for beer, so the register holds. Butler's only 'mess' uses in the whole text are 10.16, 10.22 and 10.24, all now 'brew'. His only 'brew-' words are 2.9 and 3.14 ('mischief brewing'), in other Books. There is no collision, and Butler's one word has one rendering.

Same Butler word for the same drink, in Hermes's forecast. 'mix a mess' also reads today as 'make a mess'. With 'brew', 'the meal she makes it with' now reads naturally as the barley-meal ingredient of ¶16, which is Butler's 'meal'. The rest of the sentence ('for you to drink', 'drug the meal') is untouched. No collision.

This removes the sharpest clash, slops in a golden goblet beside the silver-inlaid seat. 'but she drugged it, for she meant me mischief' still carries the drugging. 'fared onward' (ruled on separately and kept) and everything else are untouched. No collision.
